standard.title: Repeated Experiments and Simulation
standard.description: conduct repeated chance experiments and run simulations with a large number of trials using digital tools; compare predictions about outcomes with observed results, explaining the differences
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can assign probabilities and predict relative frequencies (from AC9M7P01). Students have run simulations with increasing trials (from AC9M6P02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students conduct repeated experiments and simulations to observe that relative frequencies approach theoretical probability as the number of trials increases, and explain differences between predicted and observed results.

nodes.label: Running experiments and recording results
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students conduct repeated chance experiments and record observed frequencies systematically.
nodes.minimum_width: Conduct a simple chance experiment (e.g. coin toss) for at least 20 trials and record results in a frequency table.
nodes.typical_width: Conduct experiments for increasing numbers of trials; record cumulative results; compare observed frequency to predicted frequency at each stage.
wider: Use digital tools to run simulations of the same experiment with 100, 1000, 10000 trials — record and compare results.
Investigate First Nations Australian children's instructive games as probability experiments — record and analyse outcomes.

response_modes.reason: Systematic data recording is prerequisite to any comparison between experimental and theoretical probability. Students who record inconsistently cannot see the law of large numbers pattern.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who record inconsistently cannot generate reliable relative frequencies for Node 2 comparison — without a systematic cumulative record, the convergence pattern of the law of large numbers is invisible in the data.
success_criteria: Records observed frequencies in an organised frequency table.
Calculates relative frequency from observed results.
Compares observed relative frequency to theoretical probability.

nodes.label: Law of large numbers — observed vs predicted
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students observe that relative frequencies become closer to theoretical probability as the number of trials increases, and explain why short-run results may differ from predictions.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why 3 heads from 10 coin tosses does not mean the coin is unfair, using the idea that more trials are needed.
nodes.typical_width: Use simulation data to show relative frequencies converging toward theoretical probability over many trials; describe the pattern in their own words.
wider: Investigate: how many trials are needed before the relative frequency is consistently within 5% of the theoretical probability?
Apply the law of large numbers to real contexts: insurance companies and casinos rely on this — explain how.

response_modes.reason: The law of large numbers is counter-intuitive to students who expect short runs to match predictions. Multiple experiments with different devices, each showing the same convergence pattern, build the generalised understanding.

success_criteria: States that relative frequencies approach theoretical probability as trials increase.
Explains why short-run results can differ significantly from predictions.
Does not commit the gambler's fallacy (thinking past outcomes affect future probabilities).
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Investigating how many trials are needed for stable relative frequency is a rich inquiry task — advancing students can connect this to real applications (insurance, casinos) and reason about the practical meaning of the law of large numbers.
